<main>
    <div class="article-hero">
        <span class="category-badge">Threat Intelligence</span>
        <h1 class="article-title">AI-Powered Hacker Breaches 600+ FortiGate Firewalls Across 55 Countries</h1>
        <div class="article-meta">
            <span><i class="far fa-user"></i> Harish G</span>
            <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> February 23, 2026</span>
            <span><i class="far fa-clock"></i> 15 min read</span>
        </div>
    </div>

    <div class="featured-image-container">
        <img loading="lazy" src="/images/articles/ai-hacker-fortigate-600-devices-2026.png"
            alt="AI-Powered Hacker Breaches 600+ FortiGate Firewalls" class="featured-image" width="1200"
            height="630">
    </div>

    <div class="container">

        <article class="content-wrapper">

            <a href="/articles.html" class="back-link"
                style="display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 1.5rem; color: var(--accent-cyan); text-decoration: none; font-size: 0.95rem;">
                <i class="fas fa-arrow-left"></i> Back to Articles
            </a>

            <!-- Executive Summary -->
            <div class="executive-summary">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Executive Summary</h3>
                <p><strong>What happened:</strong> Between January 11 and February 18, 2026, a Russian-speaking,
                    financially motivated threat actor used commercial generative AI tools to compromise
                    <strong>over 600 FortiGate firewall devices</strong> across <strong>55+ countries</strong>.
                </p>
                <p><strong>How:</strong> The attacker did <strong>not</strong> exploit a FortiGate zero-day. They
                    targeted exposed management interfaces with weak or default credentials lacking multi-factor
                    authentication. AI was used for attack planning, script development, and post-exploitation.</p>
                <p><strong>Who reported it:</strong> <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/"
                        target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Amazon Threat Intelligence</a>. The findings were published on February 20,
                    2026 by AWS CISO CJ Moses.</p>
                <p><strong>Confidence Level:</strong> High — based on direct observation by Amazon Threat
                    Intelligence.</p>
                <p><strong>TLP:</strong> CLEAR</p>
                <p class="source-citation">This analysis is based on the AWS Security Blog (CJ Moses, Feb 20 2026),
                    BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, Computing.co.uk, and Security Affairs reporting as of
                    February 23, 2026. Details may evolve as the investigation continues.</p>
            </div>

            <h2>1. What Actually Happened</h2>

            <p>Amazon Threat Intelligence discovered a server operated by the threat actor that contained malicious
                tools, AI-generated attack methodologies, stolen configurations from compromised devices, and custom
                tooling source code. The attacker's poor operational security (OPSEC) exposed the entire operation.
            </p>

            <p>The key finding that makes this significant: <strong>the attacker was assessed as having
                    low-to-medium technical skill</strong>. The scale of the campaign — 600+ devices across 55
                countries — was achieved almost entirely through AI augmentation of an unskilled operator.</p>

            <h3>Attack Vector: Not a Zero-Day</h3>

            <p>This is critical to understand: <strong>no FortiGate vulnerability was exploited</strong>. The
                attacker succeeded by finding FortiGate appliances with:</p>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Management interfaces exposed to the internet</strong> — a misconfiguration, not a
                    software flaw</li>
                <li><strong>Weak or default credentials</strong> on admin accounts</li>
                <li><strong>No multi-factor authentication (MFA)</strong> on admin or VPN access</li>
                <li><strong>Single-factor authentication only</strong> for SSL-VPN connections</li>
            </ul>

            <p>When the attacker encountered hardened environments (MFA enabled, management ports unexposed), they
                moved on to softer targets, according to Amazon's report.</p>

            <h2>2. The AI-Augmented Attack Chain</h2>

            <p>The attacker used <strong>multiple commercial generative AI services</strong> (the specific services
                were not named by Amazon) across every phase of the operation:</p>

            <div class="attack-timeline">
                <div class="timeline-event">
                    <div class="timeline-date">Phase 1: Reconnaissance</div>
                    <p>AI was used to generate scanning methodologies and identify exposed FortiGate management
                        interfaces across the internet. The attacker operated opportunistically — scanning for
                        low-hanging fruit rather than targeting specific organizations.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-event">
                    <div class="timeline-date">Phase 2: Credential Attacks</div>
                    <p>Default and weak credentials were tested against exposed management ports. No brute-force
                        sophistication — just basic credential stuffing augmented by AI-generated scripts.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-event">
                    <div class="timeline-date">Phase 3: Configuration Extraction</div>
                    <p>Once inside, the attacker extracted full device configurations including SSL-VPN credentials,
                        administrative usernames and passwords, firewall policies, internal network topology maps,
                        and IPsec VPN configurations.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-event">
                    <div class="timeline-date">Phase 4: AI-Assisted Parsing</div>
                    <p>Custom Python and Go scripts — generated with AI assistance — were used to parse and
                        <strong>decrypt stolen configurations</strong>. This is where the AI augmentation was most
                        impactful: the attacker lacked the skill to write these tools manually.
                    </p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-event">
                    <div class="timeline-date">Phase 5: Lateral Movement &amp; Pre-Ransomware</div>
                    <p>Using extracted VPN credentials, the attacker connected to internal networks,
                        <strong>compromised Active Directory environments</strong>, extracted credential databases,
                        and targeted <strong>backup infrastructure</strong> — a classic pre-ransomware playbook.
                    </p>
                </div>
            </div>

            <h2>3. What the AI Actually Did (and Didn't Do)</h2>

            <p>Based on Amazon's report, the AI was used for:</p>

            <table>
                <thead>
                    <tr>
                        <th>AI-Assisted Task</th>
                        <th>What It Replaced</th>
                    </tr>
                </thead>
                <tbody>
                    <tr>
                        <td>Generating attack methodologies</td>
                        <td>Manual research and planning</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>Writing Python/Go parsing scripts</td>
                        <td>Manual coding (attacker lacked this skill)</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>Decrypting FortiGate configuration files</td>
                        <td>Manual reverse engineering</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>Planning lateral movement strategies</td>
                        <td>Experienced red team knowledge</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>Creating reconnaissance frameworks</td>
                        <td>Custom scanner development</td>
                    </tr>
                </tbody>
            </table>

            <p>What the AI did <strong>not</strong> do:</p>
            <ul>
                <li>Discover or create a zero-day vulnerability</li>
                <li>Operate autonomously without human direction</li>
                <li>Bypass properly configured security controls (MFA, unexposed management ports)</li>
                <li>Execute the final ransomware payload (unclear if ransomware was deployed)</li>
            </ul>

            <div class="vuln-card">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Key Takeaway</h3>
                <p>The AI didn't make the <em>attack</em> more sophisticated. It made a <em>low-skill attacker</em>
                    capable of operating at a scale that previously required a skilled team. The attack itself was
                    basic — default credentials on exposed ports. The AI's contribution was automation, parsing, and
                    planning.</p>
            </div>

            <h2>4. Geographic and Sector Impact</h2>

            <p>The campaign was <strong>opportunistic</strong>, not targeted. Compromised devices were found across:
            </p>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>South Asia</strong></li>
                <li><strong>Latin America and Caribbean</strong></li>
                <li><strong>West Africa</strong></li>
                <li><strong>Northern Europe</strong></li>
                <li><strong>Southeast Asia</strong></li>
            </ul>
            <p>No specific industry vertical was targeted. The attacker scanned broadly and compromised whatever was
                vulnerable.</p>

            <h2>5. Detection: What to Look For</h2>

            <p>Amazon Threat Intelligence recommends auditing for the following indicators:</p>

            <div class="technical-box">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-search"></i> Detection Indicators</h3>
                <p>Check your FortiGate logs for these patterns:</p>
                <ul>
                    <li><strong>New admin accounts</strong> created after January 11, 2026 that you didn't authorize
                    </li>
                    <li><strong>New SSL-VPN user accounts</strong> that don't match HR/IT provisioning records</li>
                    <li><strong>Unusual SSH sessions</strong> to the management interface from external IPs</li>
                    <li><strong>Configuration backup exports</strong> initiated outside maintenance windows</li>
                    <li><strong>VPN connections from unexpected geographic locations</strong></li>
                </ul>
            </div>

            <div class="technical-box">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-code"></i> Example Sigma Detection Rule</h3>
                <p><em>Note: This is an example detection rule based on the reported TTPs — not Amazon's actual
                        output.</em></p>
                <pre><code class="language-yaml">title: Suspicious FortiGate Admin Account Creation

id: fg-ai-threat-2026-001 status: experimental description: Detects new admin accounts created on FortiGate devices matching the AI-assisted campaign TTPs logsource: product: fortigate service: event detection: selection: action: ‘user-add’ level: ‘super_admin’ timeframe: 5m condition: selection falsepositives: - Legitimate admin provisioning - Scheduled maintenance level: high tags: - attack.persistence - attack.t1136.001 

            <div class="technical-box">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-terminal"></i> FortiGate CLI Audit Commands</h3>
                <pre><code class="language-bash"># List all admin accounts (check for unauthorized additions)

show system admin

Review current SSL-VPN connections

diagnose vpn ssl list

Check event logs for suspicious activity

execute log filter category 1 execute log display

Review active SSL-VPN sessions for unusual IPs

get vpn ssl monitor

Check who is currently logged into the FortiGate

get system info admin status 

            <h2>6. Immediate Remediation</h2>

            <div class="success-box">
                <strong><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> IMMEDIATE ACTIONS (based on Amazon's
                    recommendations):</strong>
                <ol>
                    <li><strong>Restrict management interface access</strong> — Do not expose FortiGate management
                        ports (443/admin, 22/SSH) to the internet. Use out-of-band management or IP allowlists.</li>
                    <li><strong>Enable MFA on all admin and VPN accounts</strong> — This single control would have
                        stopped this entire campaign.</li>
                    <li><strong>Audit all admin and VPN accounts</strong> — Remove any accounts created after
                        January 11, 2026 that are not authorized.</li>
                    <li><strong>Rotate all credentials</strong> — Change admin passwords and VPN pre-shared keys.
                        Assume extracted configurations are compromised.</li>
                    <li><strong>Do not reuse VPN passwords for Active Directory</strong> — The attacker used
                        extracted VPN credentials to pivot into AD.</li>
                    <li><strong>Harden backup infrastructure</strong> — The attacker targeted backups specifically,
                        indicating pre-ransomware activity.</li>
                    <li><strong>Review firewall policies</strong> — Ensure no unauthorized rules were added during
                        the compromise.</li>
                </ol>
            </div>

            <h2>7. Why This Matters Beyond FortiGate</h2>

            <p>This campaign is the clearest documented case of <strong>AI lowering the barrier to entry for
                    cybercrime at scale</strong>. The implications are broader than one vendor:</p>

            <h3>The Skill Gap Collapse</h3>
            <p>Historically, compromising 600+ devices across 55 countries required a well-resourced team — think
                APT groups with dedicated developers, infrastructure operators, and regional specialists. This
                threat actor accomplished it as what Amazon assessed to be an <strong>individual or small
                    group</strong> with poor OPSEC and limited technical ability.</p>

            <p>The AI didn't teach the attacker to hack. It wrote the tools they couldn't write themselves. It
                planned the lateral movement they didn't know how to plan. It parsed the configurations they didn't
                know how to read.</p>

            <h3>Volume is Coming</h3>
            <p>Amazon's CJ Moses explicitly warned that <strong>AI-augmented threat activity will continue to grow
                    in volume from both skilled and unskilled adversaries throughout 2026</strong>. If a low-skill
                operator can hit 600 devices, high-skill operators with the same tools can hit an order of magnitude
                more — faster and quieter.</p>

            <h3>Basics Still Win</h3>
            <p>Here's the thing that should frustrate every security professional reading this: <strong>this entire
                    campaign fails against properly configured environments</strong>. MFA enabled? Attacker moves
                on. Management port not exposed? Attacker can't connect. VPN passwords not reused for AD? Lateral
                movement blocked.</p>

            <p>As Amazon states in their report, organizations should prioritize: patch management for perimeter
                devices, credential hygiene, network segmentation, and robust detection for post-exploitation
                indicators.</p>

            <h2>8. Sources</h2>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Primary:</strong> AWS Security Blog — CJ Moses, "Initial Access Brokers and the Emerging
                    AI-Assisted Threat Landscape" (February 20, 2026)</li>
                <li>BleepingComputer — "Hacker uses AI to breach 600 FortiGate devices across 55 countries"
                    (February 2026)</li>
                <li>The Hacker News — "AI-Powered Hacker Hits 600+ FortiGate Devices" (February 2026)</li>
                <li>Computing.co.uk — "Amazon exposes AI-augmented cyberattacker who hit 600+ FortiGate firewalls"
                    (February 2026)</li>
                <li>Security Boulevard — "AI-Assisted Threat Actor Compromises 600+ FortiGate Devices" (February
                    2026)</li>
